title: Systemic, non-opioid analgesia for severe perioperative pain

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a treatment that acts throughout the body to reliably relieve severe pain during the period around surgery without relying on opioid mechanisms. It would need to provide strong relief across varied surgical pain states, with acceptable adverse effects and enough protective sensation for patients to recognize potentially harmful injury or complications. This is a target capability; the supplied evidence does not establish that it has been achieved.

Conceptual synthesis: systemic treatment could be particularly useful when pain arises from several sites or when a local or regional nerve block is insufficient or impractical. The goal is broader than demonstrating that a particular non-opioid drug relieves pain after one operation. It requires dependable clinical benefit across defined surgical settings, together with evidence about recovery, rescue medication and harms.

significance.text: Conditional significance: a broadly effective systemic treatment with substantially lower risks of respiratory depression and dependence than opioids could substantially change perioperative pain care. It could reduce the amount of opioid treatment needed while expanding options for patients whose pain is inadequately controlled by other approaches. The revolutionary feature would be the combination of strong analgesia, useful clinical breadth and a better safety profile.

Conditional downstream possibilities include easier participation in postoperative rehabilitation and less disruption of recovery by pain or treatment-related adverse effects. These benefits would need direct measurement: a reduction in a pain score does not itself establish better mobility, function or overall recovery.

Limits on the impact claim: reducing perioperative opioid exposure would not by itself end addiction or resolve the opioid crisis. Effectiveness for acute surgical pain would also not establish effectiveness for chronic pain or prevention of chronic postsurgical pain. The goal does not assume zero addiction risk, zero adverse effects or elimination of the need for rescue treatment.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unsolved capability, as framed by the supplied research and review, is reliable, strong systemic analgesia across varied severe surgical pain states while retaining an acceptable safety margin and useful protective sensation. The supplied material does not independently establish how much of this gap remains open today. Nevertheless, it identifies a coherent scientific challenge: different surgical injuries and pain mechanisms may respond differently to the same intervention, so success in one procedure cannot establish broad applicability.

Scientific and engineering synthesis: a successful intervention would need to suppress clinically important pain strongly enough to support recovery without excessively impairing protective responses or producing unacceptable effects elsewhere in the body. Its dosing, duration and tolerability would need to remain useful across the intended surgical populations. A promising molecular mechanism is therefore only part of the breakthrough; dependable clinical performance and practical administration are also required.

The comparative evidence presents a separate barrier. Superiority to placebo establishes a different proposition from comparability to effective opioid-based care. Establishing broad clinical usefulness would require adequately powered comparisons, prespecified definitions of meaningful benefit, transparent accounting for rescue medication and explicit assessment of function, protective sensation and harms. Short trials cannot settle dependence-related outcomes or the safety of repeated use.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies suzetrigine, a non-opioid NaV1.8 inhibitor, as a relevant clinical advance. It attributes to Todd Bertoch, Dominick D’Aunno, Jessica McCoun and colleagues an Anesthesiology article dated 1 June 2025 describing two phase 3 randomized trials. According to that research summary, suzetrigine reduced pain versus placebo over 48 hours after abdominoplasty or bunionectomy, but did not demonstrate superiority to the studied hydrocodone/acetaminophen regimen on the first key secondary endpoint. These details are retained as reported findings, with the verification limitation described below.

Access limits materially constrain confidence in that account. The research says that an indexed abstract was available and direct full-text access encountered a browser check. The subsequent evidence review, however, found only a cookie interstitial in the retained artifact, with no inspectable abstract or trial results. It therefore could not verify the article’s identity, date, trial design, procedures, 48-hour outcome or comparator findings from document content. The source index’s saved and verified flags do not resolve this discrepancy. This is a limitation of the available evidence record, not evidence that the reported clinical results are false.

Interpretive synthesis: even if the reported findings are confirmed, they would establish a narrower achievement than the proposed innovation. Pain reduction versus placebo in two procedures would not establish efficacy across diverse major operations. Failure to demonstrate superiority over the specified opioid combination would establish neither equivalence nor noninferiority, and would not characterize comparisons with every opioid regimen. The reported 48-hour efficacy window also cannot establish the absence of important harms or outcomes after repeated treatment.

The supplied review contains no bounded search record establishing subsequent developments or the state of the field through its referenced 1 November 2026 cutoff. The source index records retrieval on 11 November 2026, but the retained interstitial supplies no clinical update. The dated 2025 report is therefore preserved without treating it as a complete account of current clinical availability, regulatory status or later evidence.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independent randomized trials across diverse major operations should show clinically meaningful pain relief and functional recovery comparable to effective opioid-based care. Protocols should define the intended populations, treatment setting, comparators and clinically justified comparability margins in advance, with adequate statistical power. These are proposed criteria for assessing the innovation, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Independent trials demonstrate opioid-comparable analgesia and recovery across major operations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurements should include pain at rest and during activity, rescue treatment, functional recovery and preservation of protective sensation. Rescue medication should be reported so that apparent success cannot conceal substantial reliance on additional opioids. Safety assessment should explicitly address respiratory events, dependence-related outcomes and other clinically important adverse effects, with follow-up appropriate to each outcome.
completion_criteria.label: Report analgesic outcomes, rescue opioid reliance and comprehensive safety assessments

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: benefits should be reproduced by independent investigators and across relevant patient groups, with usable dosing and administration requirements. The resulting claim should state where treatment works, where evidence remains limited and when additional analgesia is needed. Finite trials can demonstrate breadth across tested settings; they cannot prove literal universality or zero risk. Repeated use, chronic-pain treatment and prevention of chronic postsurgical pain would require separate evidence and longer follow-up.
completion_criteria.label: Independently reproduce benefits across patient groups and state treatment boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ANS-03, “A broadly applicable, pain-selective surgical nerve block,” shares the goal of strong analgesia with selective preservation of useful function. Its focus is a local or regional block, whereas ANS-07 concerns systemic treatment. The approaches could complement one another, especially when a block provides incomplete coverage. ANS-09, “Mechanism-based prevention of chronic postsurgical pain,” addresses whether persistent pain can be prevented; acute perioperative relief alone would not establish that outcome.

Roster-based synthesis: ANS-01, “A causal theory of anesthetic-induced unconsciousness,” and ANS-02, “A reliable real-time monitor of conscious experience during anesthesia,” concern consciousness and its assessment. ANS-04, “Surgical unconsciousness with preserved breathing and circulatory control,” concerns achieving unconsciousness while maintaining vital physiological control. ANS-07 concerns pain relief: effective analgesia does not by itself establish unconsciousness, absence of conscious experience or adequate conditions for surgery.

Roster-based synthesis: ANS-06, “Broad, active reversal of general anesthesia,” concerns recovery from the anesthetized state, whereas ANS-07 concerns controlling pain around surgery. ANS-10, “Mechanism-guided anesthesia to prevent postoperative brain dysfunction,” addresses a separate recovery outcome. Pain control and treatment-related adverse effects could interact with these goals, but analgesic efficacy would not establish either reliable anesthetic reversal or prevention of brain dysfunction.

Roster-based synthesis: ANS-05, “A radically accessible, resilient anesthesia platform for essential surgery,” shares an interest in practical delivery of surgical care. A useful systemic analgesic could contribute to such a platform, but its cost, availability and administration requirements would need separate evaluation. ANS-08, “Reliable rescue oxygenation in the difficult airway,” addresses an airway emergency capability. Lower respiratory risk from an analgesic would not establish the ability to rescue oxygenation when an airway crisis occurs.

The discrepancy between the research’s reported access to an indexed abstract and the review’s retained artifact remains unresolved.
The supplied evidence does not establish the present-day extent of the clinical gap, later trial results, regulatory status or clinical availability.

The current record does not establish broad efficacy across major operations, comparative efficacy against other opioid regimens, preservation of protective sensation, functional recovery or longer-term harms.
The proposed comparability margins, trial populations, follow-up durations and practical administration requirements require specification; none is presented as an established standard.

brief.title: Strong pain relief around surgery without opioids
possible: People facing major surgery could get dependable relief from severe pain through a treatment that works throughout the body without opioids, drugs such as hydrocodone. It would work across different operations while preserving enough sensation to warn of injury or complications.
why: Patients could need fewer opioids, with lower risks of dangerously slowed breathing and dependence. Strong pain relief with fewer treatment side effects could also make rehabilitation easier, especially for people whose pain other treatments do not adequately control.

sources.who: Todd Bertoch, Dominick D’Aunno, Jessica McCoun and colleagues
sources.showed: Suzetrigine, an oral drug that blocks a protein involved in pain signals, reduced pain after tummy tuck or bunion surgery compared with an inactive treatment. It did not outperform hydrocodone combined with acetaminophen.
sources.quote: As compared with placebo, suzetrigine reduced moderate-to-severe acute pain over 48 h after abdominoplasty or bunionectomy.
sources.cited_for: A drug acting without opioids can relieve substantial pain after specific operations.
sources.not_established: These trials do not establish equivalent relief to opioid care, broad surgical usefulness or long-term safety.

sources.showed: After impacted wisdom-tooth removal, ibuprofen with acetaminophen gave better early pain relief and greater satisfaction than hydrocodone with acetaminophen. Across the full recovery period, pain was no worse.
sources.quote: At no time did hydrocodone outperform the nonopioid.
sources.cited_for: Existing medicines without opioids can match or exceed an opioid combination in a defined surgical setting.
sources.not_established: Success after wisdom-tooth removal does not establish dependable relief across major operations.

sources.showed: In a small trial after lung surgery through small incisions, acetaminophen with ibuprofen given into a vein reduced opioid use and most pain scores. Hospital stays did not shorten.
sources.quote: All pain scores except for coughing at 48 h post-surgery were significantly lower in the intervention group compared to the controls.
sources.cited_for: Medicines without opioids can reduce the need for opioids after major surgery.
sources.not_established: Patients still received opioids, so the trial does not establish adequate relief without them or better overall recovery.

sources.who: Qiucheng Zhao, Yang Wang, Fujian Huang, Zhaoyang Xiao and Xiaoyu Xu
sources.showed: A single-hospital trial in older adults used medicines without opioids during abdominal surgery. Patients had less nausea and earlier bowel recovery, but waking took longer and high blood pressure during surgery was more frequent.
sources.quote: it did not result in a clinically meaningful improvement in overall postoperative recovery
sources.cited_for: Reducing opioid use can improve some outcomes while introducing other harms.
sources.not_established: Avoiding opioids during surgery did not establish better overall recovery or eliminate opioid use afterward.

shown: Researchers have achieved pain relief without opioids in particular procedures and reduced opioid use in others. The strongest results remain tied to specific operations and treatment plans; dependable relief across varied major operations has yet to be established.
missing: Independent trials have yet to establish strong pain relief and recovery comparable to effective opioid care across varied major operations.
Broadly effective treatment has yet to demonstrate that patients retain warning sensations for injury and complications.
Longer follow-up has yet to establish acceptable risks of breathing problems, dependence and repeated treatment.

milestones.label: Independent trials find comparable relief and recovery across major operations
milestones.explanation: Independent randomized trials would have to show pain relief and functional recovery comparable to effective opioid care across diverse major operations. This would establish clinical breadth beyond isolated procedures.

milestones.label: Pain relief, additional opioid use and safety are measured together
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to measure pain at rest and during activity, extra opioid use, recovery, warning sensations and harms with suitable follow-up. This would reveal whether apparent success hides opioid reliance or unacceptable risks.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce benefits and define treatment boundaries
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce benefits across patient groups with practical dosing and clear limits on where treatment works. This would establish dependable use and when additional pain relief remains necessary.

uncertain: How close must pain relief and recovery be to opioid care to count as comparable?
Which patient groups, operations and follow-up periods would establish enough breadth and safety?

page.title: Systemic nonopioid analgesia for severe postoperative pain
page.definition: An oral or injected drug distributed through the bloodstream replaces opioid treatment for severe postoperative pain in a defined surgical population, with pain control comparable to an opioid regimen and without using an opioid mechanism.

goal.need: A US claims study of previously opioid-naive adults undergoing elective surgery in 2013–2014 found persistent prescription exposure after both minor and major procedures. All 36,177 surgical patients had filled a perioperative opioid prescription. Prescription fulfillment does not diagnose addiction.

figures.caption: Opioid prescription fulfillment 90–180 days after surgery
figures.note: Observational results from privately insured US adults; these percentages do not establish that surgery caused subsequent opioid use.

completion.title: FDA labeling recognizes opioid replacement in a specified postoperative pain setting.
completion.criterion: FDA-authorized labeling describes opioid replacement by a systemic nonopioid analgesic in a specified postoperative setting: statistically significant elimination of opioid need where opioids are routinely required, with analgesia comparable to or better than the opioid comparator. FDA specifies no fixed responder percentage or comparability margin.
completion.set_by: FDA, Development of Non-Opioid Analgesics for Acute Pain, May 2026 draft guidance, section III.B.2.a; nonbinding recommendations.
completion.threshold_quote: eliminates the need for an opioid analgesic in a statistically significant number of patients
completion.basis: FDA’s opioid-replacement claim tests the capability defined here. Ketorolac already has an opioid-level indication, and FDA approved suzetrigine on 30 January 2025. Suzetrigine’s original label establishes placebo-controlled efficacy; it contains no opioid-replacement claim.

milestones.title: Preclinical evidence supports human testing of a systemic nonopioid candidate under an effective IND.
milestones.criterion: Preclinical pharmacology and toxicology support an assessment that a candidate is reasonably safe for initial human testing; its investigational new drug application (IND) permits the planned study to proceed. Manufacturing and protocol information are also required. Laboratory results published in 2023 showed VX-548 had at least 31,000-fold selectivity for NaV1.8, a sodium channel involved in pain signaling, over other NaV subtypes. Its subsequent phase 3 protocol identifies IND 146185.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Investigational New Drug Application requirements; the safety assessment depends on the candidate and proposed human exposure.
milestones.threshold_quote: Nonclinical data to permit an assessment as to whether the product is reasonably safe for initial testing in humans.

milestones.title: A systemic nonopioid candidate is administered to people in a phase 1 study.
milestones.criterion: An investigational systemic nonopioid is administered to human participants in phase 1, with assessment of exposure and dose-related adverse effects. FDA sets no universal participant count or tolerated dose. FDA's 2025 review records suzetrigine's first-in-human study VX19-548-001: 40 healthy adults aged 18–55 years, including 32 receiving suzetrigine and 8 placebo, with single doses of 7.5–65 mg.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Drug Development and Review Definitions, Phase I Clinical Studies.
milestones.threshold_quote: Phase 1 includes the initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans.

milestones.title: A systemic nonopioid improves 48-hour postoperative pain relief versus placebo in phase 2.
milestones.criterion: The registered phase 2 suzetrigine studies compared 48-hour pain relief with placebo at a nominal two-sided significance level of 0.05. SPID48 integrates improvement from baseline on a 0–10 pain scale over 48 hours; higher values indicate more relief. Reported in 2023, the trials enrolled 303 abdominoplasty and 274 bunionectomy participants. High-dose differences were 37.8 pain-score-hours (95% CI 9.2–66.4) and 36.8 (4.6–69.0), respectively. These confidence intervals were not adjusted for multiple comparisons.
milestones.set_by: Vertex Pharmaceuticals, registered phase 2 protocols NCT05034952 and NCT04977336, as described in the trial publication; these endpoints concern abdominoplasty and bunionectomy.

milestones.title: A systemic nonopioid meets a prespecified 48-hour pain endpoint in confirmatory postoperative trials.
milestones.criterion: Meet the prespecified primary efficacy endpoint in randomized confirmatory trials. Protocol VX22-548-105 tests SPID48 superiority to placebo at two-sided α=0.05. Published on 21 March 2025, suzetrigine trials enrolled 1,118 abdominoplasty and 1,073 bunionectomy participants. Differences were 48.4 pain-score-hours (95% CI 33.6–63.1; P<0.0001) and 29.3 (14.0–44.6; P=0.0002). Neither established superiority to hydrocodone/acetaminophen 5/325 mg every 6 hours. This does not establish noninferiority.
milestones.set_by: Vertex Pharmaceuticals, protocol VX22-548-105, version 4.0, section 12.3.3.3; the quoted testing rule was written for abdominoplasty.
milestones.threshold_quote: Each endpoint will be tested in the following order at the 2-sided significance level of 0.05:

milestones.title: A nonopioid regimen keeps postoperative dental pain within 1 point of an opioid regimen.
milestones.criterion: In OARS, the upper limit of the two-sided 98.75% confidence interval for nonopioid minus opioid pain scores must be below 1.0 point for each of four postoperative periods. Of 1,888 randomized adults, 1,815 underwent eligible third-molar surgery; regimens were ibuprofen/acetaminophen 400/500 mg or hydrocodone/acetaminophen 5/300 mg. The 2025 report found an across-recovery difference of −0.20 points (98.75% CI −0.45 to 0.05), with superiority on days 1–2. Rescue analgesia was required by 26 (2.89%) versus 54 (6.07%). This margin applies to this dental trial.
milestones.set_by: OARS investigators, registered dental-surgery protocol NCT04452344, with its prespecified analysis described in the published report.

milestones.title: A systemic nonopioid eliminates postoperative opioid need while providing comparable pain control.
milestones.criterion: Controlled evidence establishes opioid elimination in a statistically significant patient group where opioids are routinely needed, with comparable pain control. Reduced consumption alone does not meet this condition. In 2024, intravenous acetaminophen/ibuprofen reduced 24-hour opioid consumption after thoracic surgery in 96 participants by a median 100 µg intravenous fentanyl equivalents. In 2026, opioid-free anesthesia in 200 randomized older abdominal-surgery patients reduced postoperative opioid use; the 24-hour recovery-score difference was 4 points (95% CI 2–8), below the trial's clinical-significance threshold. Neither establishes complete postoperative opioid replacement.
milestones.set_by: FDA, May 2026 draft guidance, sections III.B.2 and III.B.2.a; nonbinding recommendations.
milestones.threshold_quote: the non-opioid and opioid have comparable effects on pain.

not_found: No external criterion specifying how many major operations establish broad surgical efficacy was located in FDA guidance or NIH HEAL programme documents.
No acceptance threshold for preserved protective sensation was located in those documents.
No explicit grant of the defined opioid-replacement labeling claim was located in the ketorolac and suzetrigine labels inspected.

results.finding: In phase 3 trials, suzetrigine improved SPID48 versus placebo by 48.4 points after abdominoplasty (n=1,118) and 29.3 after bunionectomy (n=1,073).
results.detail: Both trials met their prespecified primary endpoint. Neither established superiority or noninferiority to hydrocodone/acetaminophen.

results.finding: After abdominoplasty (n=1,118), the SPID48 difference between suzetrigine and hydrocodone/acetaminophen was 6.6 pain-score-hours.
results.detail: The trial compared a nonopioid with an opioid regimen, but did not establish noninferiority or statistically significant elimination of postoperative opioid need. Ibuprofen rescue was permitted, and participants could discontinue treatment for alternative medication.

results.finding: In 1,815 dental surgery patients, the across-recovery pain difference was −0.20 points.
results.detail: The upper 98.75% confidence bound was below the 1-point margin in all four postoperative periods. The nonopioid regimen was ibuprofen/acetaminophen; the comparator was hydrocodone/acetaminophen.
results.quote:

results.finding: Among 1,815 dental surgery patients, 26 in the nonopioid group required rescue analgesia.
results.detail: Pain control was comparable, but opioid rescue was available and used. The trial does not establish complete elimination of postoperative opioid need in a patient group where opioids are routinely needed.
results.quote:
Participants not taking opioids had less need for rescue analgesic (n ¼ 26 [2.89%] vs n ¼ 54

results.finding: In 90 analyzed thoracic surgery patients, IV acetaminophen/ibuprofen reduced 24-hour analgesic consumption by a median 100 µg IV fentanyl equivalents.
results.detail: The trial randomized 96 patients and analyzed 90. Both groups received postoperative fentanyl; reduced opioid consumption does not establish opioid elimination or comparable pain control without opioids.
results.quote:

results.finding: In 195 older abdominal-surgery patients, opioid-free anesthesia reduced mean 48-hour sufentanil consumption by 18 µg.
results.detail: Both groups received postoperative sufentanil by patient-controlled analgesia, so opioid need was not eliminated. Pain scores were broadly similar, but the secondary outcomes were not adjusted for multiple comparisons.
results.quote: OFA reduced the incidence of PONV during the first 72 postoperative hours and modestly reduced postoperative opioid consumption.

results.finding: Suzetrigine inhibited pain signals in 10 of 17 human sensory neurons from three donors.
results.detail: The study provides preclinical pharmacology and animal safety evidence, but does not establish an effective IND or provide the required manufacturing and protocol information.

results.finding: In 303 abdominoplasty participants, high-dose VX-548 improved SPID48 versus placebo by 37.8 pain-score-hours.
results.detail: The 95% confidence interval was 9.2 to 66.4; confidence intervals were not adjusted for multiple comparisons. The separate bunionectomy trial also favored high-dose VX-548 over placebo.

results.finding: In 132 analyzed gynecological laparoscopy patients, intravenous esketamine–dexmedetomidine provided non-inferior pain control versus sufentanil (p = 0.008).
results.detail: The postoperative regimen was opioid-free, but the paper describes this surgical population as having moderate acute pain and relatively minor surgical trauma. It does not establish replacement for severe postoperative pain. Patients also received intraoperative opioids and routinely received NSAIDs.
results.quote: In this randomized controlled trial of patients undergoing gynaecological laparoscopic surgery, postoperative opioid-free analgesia combining esketamine and dexmedetomidine was non-inferior to sufentanil-based opioid analgesia for pain control during the first 48 h postoperatively.

results.finding: In 315 orthopedic surgery patients, 18.5% assigned to the opioid-free pathway required breakthrough opioids.
results.detail: The randomized trial found noninferior 24-hour pain control overall, but the pathway combined systemic drugs with regional or neuraxial anesthesia, and some patients required opioids. It did not establish that a systemic nonopioid drug alone replaced postoperative opioids with comparable pain control.
